analysis.one_liner: Bars health insurers and employers from using people's genetic information against them or their families.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on July 1, 1999 with 16 Democratic cosponsors and never received a hearing, vote, or any further action in the Senate committee it was assigned to before Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it illegal for health insurers to deny coverage, raise premiums, or demand genetic tests based on a person's genetic information or family medical history. It would have also made it illegal for employers, employment agencies, unions, and apprenticeship programs to hire, fire, or classify workers based on the same information. It gave people the right to sue in federal or state court, with attorney's fees and expert costs paid by violators, and let the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission enforce the employment rules. States with stronger protections could keep them, since the bill did not override tougher state laws.
analysis.who_benefits: People with a genetic test result, a family history of disease, or family members of someone who had genetic testing or genetic counseling — that is, anyone whose genes suggest a future risk of illness. They could get genetic tests and counseling without fearing they would lose their health coverage, pay higher premiums, or be passed over for a job. Workers in jobs with toxic exposures would also gain, because the bill let employers do genetic monitoring only with written consent and only if the employer saw results in anonymous, aggregate form.

how_it_helps.text: Health insurers could not deny enrollment or adjust premiums in the individual market, deny eligibility to a group, or adjust group rates based on predictive genetic information or on requests for genetic services, and could not ask or require anyone to take a genetic test [S2] [S3].

Insurers could not collect, buy, or disclose predictive genetic information without the person's written authorization, and could not share it with the person's employer, other insurers, or companies like the Medical Information Bureau that compile insurance records [S2] [S3].

Employers, employment agencies, labor organizations, and apprenticeship programs could not refuse to hire, discharge, or discriminate against anyone because of predictive genetic information, and could not request or collect that information except in narrow cases like consented workplace genetic monitoring where the employer sees only anonymous aggregate results [S2] [S3].

Medicare supplemental (Medigap) policies could not be denied, conditioned, or priced based on predictive genetic information, extending the same protections to seniors buying supplemental coverage [S3].

Victims could sue in federal or state court for any appropriate relief including attorney's fees and expert witness costs, civil penalties applied, and states were free to keep or adopt stronger genetic privacy and nondiscrimination laws [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers would lose the ability to use genetic information in underwriting, their traditional tool for pricing risk, and would bear enforcement and penalty exposure. Employers would face compliance costs and lose the option of genetic screening of workers or applicants. If genetic risks could no longer be priced into individual premiums, the cost of covering people with elevated genetic risk would be spread across other policyholders.

drawbacks.text: Barring insurers in the individual market from pricing genetic risk could raise premiums for everyone else in that market, since costs from higher-risk enrollees get spread across the pool [S2].
Employers would bear the cost of treating genetic information as confidential medical records and could face lawsuits, with violators potentially paying attorney's fees and expert costs [S2] [S3].

The bill did leave carve-outs: plans could still request genetic information to pay claims when the claim would otherwise be denied, and employers could offer genetic services or workplace genetic monitoring with the employee's written consent [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections were broad and enforceable — they covered group and individual insurance, Medicare supplement policies, and employment, and let stronger state laws stand. The main cost falls on insurers' underwriting flexibility and employer compliance, with some premium-spreading in the individual market. That is a real but ordinary trade-off of nondiscrimination rules, not a design flaw. The bill's major limitation was that it died in committee, so none of these benefits ever took effect.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate's health committee, which never held a hearing or vote on it, and it died there when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Tom Daschle, joined by original cosponsors Sens. Harkin, Dodd, and Kennedy, introduced the Genetic Nondiscrimination in Health Insurance and Employment Act of 1999 on July 1, 1999 [S1] [S3].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day it was introduced [S5].
No committee markup, hearing action, floor vote, or further step appears in its action history after that referral [S5].
Sixteen senators cosponsored the bill, all of them Democrats [S4].
The 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, and bills not passed by then die and must be reintroduced from scratch in the next Congress [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers were better off because the bill never advanced: they kept full freedom to use genetic information and family medical history in underwriting and employment decisions, with no federal floor beyond existing law. People with genetic disease risks remained unprotected at the federal level.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employers kept the status quo

for.name: Sen. Tom Daschle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 1, 1999 and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Sens. Harkin, Dodd, and Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as original cosponsors.

for.name: 16 of 100 Senators
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 16 cosponsors were Democrats.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican in the 106th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action on it — no markup, no hearing listed, no report to the floor — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.role: Majority party controlling the Senate and its committee agenda
against.what_they_did: None of the bill's 16 cosponsors were Republicans, and the majority party allowed the bill to sit in committee without action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 16 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republicans signed on, and the Republican-run committee never acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would have stripped insurers' ability to deny coverage, raise premiums, or require genetic tests based on predictive genetic information in group, individual, and Medigap markets, and barred them from collecting or sharing that data. Insurers' underwriting interest ran directly against protections people with genetic risk needed.

The bill would have made genetic discrimination in hiring, firing, and workplace classification unlawful and restricted employers' ability to request or buy workers' genetic information, with lawsuit and fee exposure for violations.
By removing the fear that a genetic test result could cost someone their coverage or job, the bill would have made people more willing to seek genetic tests and counseling.

industries.industry: Medical data compilers such as the Medical Information Bureau
industries.note: The bill specifically barred plans and insurers from disclosing genetic information to organizations that compile and disseminate insurance information, cutting off a data channel they profit from.
